explanation.what_it_is: Copper is an essential trace mineral found in foods like shellfish, nuts, seeds, and whole grains. Your body needs only small amounts, but copper is a critical cofactor in dozens of enzymes that power energy production, collagen formation, and antioxidant defense.
explanation.how_it_works: Copper works primarily as a component of metalloenzymes—proteins that require copper to function. It helps cytochrome c oxidase drive aerobic respiration in mitochondria, supports lysyl oxidase in collagen and elastin cross-linking, and is central to superoxide dismutase, a major antioxidant enzyme. It also plays roles in iron metabolism, myelin formation in nerves, and regulation of immune signaling molecules. Because of these broad roles, copper deficiency impairs multiple body systems.

proven_benefits.note: Human evidence (28 studies) shows copper supports immune cell activity and antibody production, though the clinical magnitude of benefit in well-nourished people remains modest.
Human evidence (29 studies) indicates copper influences inflammatory signaling pathways, with potential relevance to chronic inflammatory states, but effects are moderate in magnitude.
Human evidence (22 studies) links copper to endothelial function, arterial elasticity, and cholesterol metabolism, though clinical outcomes in prevention remain incompletely understood.

promising_benefits.note: Early human evidence (30 studies) suggests copper may influence gut barrier integrity and microbiota, but studies are mostly small or mechanistic; clinical benefit is not yet established.
Preliminary human data (36 studies) point to copper's role in neurotransmitter synthesis and stress signaling, but causality in anxiety disorders is unproven and inconsistent across studies.

explanation.emerging_research: Recent work is exploring copper's role in neuroinflammation and neurodegenerative disease, as well as its interaction with zinc balance in aging and immunity. Some research suggests dysregulation of copper metabolism may relate to neurodevelopmental conditions, but these findings remain exploratory in humans and require validation.
explanation.caveats: Copper is essential but narrow therapeutic window—excess copper can cause toxicity (nausea, liver damage), while deficiency is rare in balanced diets. Do not supplement beyond dietary needs without medical guidance. Quality and bioavailability of copper supplements vary; whole food sources (shellfish, legumes, seeds) are preferred when possible.
